title: Packers Eye Jonathan Taylor Trade After Josh Jacobs Update Boosts Likelihood, Sports Illustrated Reports
body:
Green Bay’s front office has moved from speculation to concrete interest, signaling that a trade for Indianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor could soon become a reality. The push for the former Ohio State star intensified after new concerns emerged surrounding the Colts’ own backfield, particularly the lingering injury questions surrounding Josh Jacobs. Sources close to the Packers confirmed that the team has opened formal channels with Indianapolis, exploring options that would bring Taylor’s proven rushing prowess to Lambeau Field as the franchise seeks to revitalize a ground game that has struggled to find consistency this season.

The Packers entered the 2024 campaign with high expectations for a balanced offense, yet their rushing attack has been hampered by injuries and underperformance. Running back Aaron Jones, the team’s primary ball carrier, has missed significant time, while rookie AJ Duncan has yet to make a lasting impact. In the first nine games, Green Bay has averaged just 3.7 yards per carry, ranking near the bottom of the league. Adding a player of Taylor’s caliber—who amassed 1,811 rushing yards and 11 touchdowns last season—could instantly lift the team’s ground game, providing a reliable workhorse and opening up play‑action opportunities for quarterback Jordan Love.

Taylor’s value on the market has surged after a breakout 2023‑24 season in which he posted a 4.9 yards‑per‑carry average and became one of only two backs to eclipse the 1,500‑yard mark. His blend of vision, burst, and durability makes him a rare commodity in a league where elite running backs are increasingly scarce. For the Colts, however, the prospect of moving Taylor is complicated by contractual considerations and the need to replace his production. Indianapolis is reportedly weighing offers that include a combination of draft capital and roster players, with particular interest in securing a high‑round pick that could accelerate their rebuild.

The emerging “Jacobs factor” has added urgency to the trade talks. Jacobs, the Colts’ former first‑round pick, has been sidelined with a lingering ankle issue, prompting doubts about his ability to shoulder the workload that Taylor would leave behind. Colts executives have hinted that they may be open to a deal that mitigates the risk of a single‑back dependency, especially if they can acquire assets to diversify their offensive weapons. Green Bay’s willingness to engage now suggests they view Taylor as a long‑term solution rather than a stop‑gap, potentially offering a multi‑year contract that aligns with the team’s salary‑cap strategy.

From a strategic standpoint, the acquisition would represent a shift in Green Bay’s offensive philosophy. Head coach Matt LaFleur has traditionally favored a pass‑heavy scheme, leveraging the arm talent of Love and the receiving depth of Davante Adams and Marquez Valdes‑Scantling. Yet the league’s recent trend toward balanced attacks—exemplified by teams like the Dallas Cowboys and the Baltimore Ravens—underscores the value of a dominant rusher in controlling tempo and keeping defenses honest. Taylor’s presence could also alleviate pressure on the offensive line, which has struggled with consistency, by allowing more predictable blocking schemes and reducing the frequency of blitz calls.

Looking ahead, the next few days will be crucial for both franchises. If the Packers can finalize a deal that satisfies Indianapolis’ demand for draft assets while staying within Green Bay’s cap constraints, they could unveil Taylor at the upcoming press conference, signaling a decisive move to reshape their offensive identity. For the Colts, securing the right return could accelerate their rebuilding timeline, giving them flexibility to explore emerging talents at running back or pivot to a more pass‑oriented approach. Regardless of the outcome, the potential trade underscores how quickly NFL fortunes can change and highlights the strategic calculus teams employ when balancing immediate needs against long‑term planning.
